screens.title: LVM with Ansible — Part 1
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we focus on the first layer of LVM automation: turning raw disks into Physical Volumes and grouping them into Volume Groups using Ansible. You will understand what a Physical Volume is, why a Volume Group acts like a pooled storage device, and how Ansible’s community. general. lvg module simplifies creation and extension. We will use concrete playbook examples and show how the module implicitly initializes devices, what idempotent behavior means in practice, and the verification commands used after a run. This matters because managing storage by hand is error-prone; automating LVM saves time and reduces risk when adding capacity, especially across many servers. As you move through the lesson, notice the mapping from raw disks to PVs to a VG to create flexible Logical Volumes later. A common pitfall is initializing a disk that already holds data; we will highlight safety checks and verification steps so you can automate confidently. By the end of this chapter you will be able to write a minimal Ansible task to form a VG from two disks and verify the outcome.

Module 04 › Chapter 4.4 › LVM with Ansible
Logical Volume Management with Ansible — Part 1
Automate Physical Volumes and Volume Groups so you can allocate flexible, resizable storage programmatically.
In this lesson
Definitions of PVs and VGs, an Ansible playbook walkthrough for creating a VG, verification commands, and safety best practices to avoid data loss.
Coming up
A reproducible task using community.general.lvg that will initialize disks as PVs when necessary and create or extend the named VG.
Quick topics
Physical Volume (PV)
A raw disk or partition initialized for LVM use.
Volume Group (VG)
A pool of PVs providing a single storage space to create LVs.
Ansible lvg
community.general.lvg initializes devices and manages VG creation or extension idempotently.
Visual map
/dev/sdb, /dev/sdc
raw disks to initialize
Physical Volumes (PV)
initialized by lvg when needed
Volume Group (VG)
a pooled block device for Logical Volumes
Start tip
Confirm device names with lsblk and ensure disks are unmounted and empty. Initializing a PV will overwrite headers and may destroy data.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain the three core LVM concepts, create Physical Volumes and Volume Groups using Ansible, extend an existing Volume Group by adding disks, and reason about safety and verification steps. Each objective ties a practical skill to a safety check or verification technique so you automate confidently. For example, you'll learn that marking a disk as a Physical Volume alters its on-disk header, which is why verifying the device with lsblk and pvdisplay is necessary before running a playbook. You will also practice writing a minimal community. general. lvg task that is idempotent and can be run repeatedly without unintended changes. Finally, you will recognize common mistakes such as trying to add a mounted or in-use device, and you will learn the commands to inspect the resulting VG so you can confirm success. These skills let you scale storage changes across many hosts reliably.

screens.title: What is a Physical Volume (PV)?
screens.narratorSegment: A Physical Volume, or PV, is a raw disk or partition that has been prepared for use by LVM. When you initialize a disk as a PV you write an LVM header that identifies the device to the volume management layer; after that the device is not used directly for a traditional filesystem. PVs are the atomic units that Volume Groups pool together. For example, marking /dev/sdb and /dev/sdc as PVs allows you to combine their capacity into a single VG. This is useful when a single filesystem needs more capacity than a single disk. A common misconception is that a PV is a filesystem or mountable device — it is not. It is an LVM-managed block that must be part of a VG to host a Logical Volume. A practical example: you discover two unpartitioned disks on a VM. You run an Ansible task that references those devices; the community. general. lvg module will initialize them as PVs if necessary. Always verify devices with lsblk or pvdisplay before automating to avoid overwriting important data. Key takeaway: PVs convert physical disks or partitions into LVM-managed capacity and are the first step in creating flexible, resizable volumes.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.4 › Physical Volume
Definition
Physical Volume (PV)
A raw disk or partition prepared with an LVM header. It cannot be used directly for filesystems once initialized.
Analogy
Think of each PV as a brick that can be combined with other bricks to build a storage wall (the VG).
Common misconception
A PV is not mountable and is not a filesystem. It is a block device allocated into a VG to host logical volumes.
Key Takeaway

Initializing a PV writes metadata to the device header. Verify with lsblk and pvdisplay before initializing to avoid data loss.

Example
You have two unpartitioned disks, /dev/sdb and /dev/sdc. Each will become a PV when initialized and then can be added to a VG to provide combined capacity.
Check devices
Run lsblk to confirm devices are present and unmounted before automation.
Verify PV
Use pvdisplay on the target host after playbook runs to confirm PV creation and attributes.
Pro tip
Label devices consistently on VMs so your playbooks target the intended disks and reduce risk.

screens.title: What is a Volume Group (VG)?
screens.narratorSegment: A Volume Group, or VG, aggregates one or more Physical Volumes into a single storage pool. Think of a VG as a virtual super-disk: it exposes the combined capacity of its member PVs so you can create Logical Volumes of arbitrary size up to the total free space. This pooling is the key advantage of LVM because it lets you grow storage for an application without being constrained to single physical disks. For example, if you add /dev/sdc to an existing VG that already includes /dev/sdb, the VG capacity increases and you can extend LVs carved from it. An important property is that VGs are extensible: adding PVs increases total free space. Another practical note is that operations against VGs in automation should be idempotent; Ansible's community. general. lvg module will create the VG if missing and add devices that are not yet members. Remember that adding a PV to a VG writes to the device header, so the safety checks for PVs apply here as well. Finally, a misconception is thinking a VG automatically balances data across disks in the same way as RAID; LVM pools capacity but does not provide redundancy unless configured with mirroring or higher-level replication. Key takeaway: VGs give you a single namespace for capacity and make resizing and allocation far simpler.

keyIdea.title: VG core idea
keyIdea.text: A VG pools multiple PVs into one storage space from which Logical Volumes are allocated and resized.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.4 › Volume Group
Definition
Volume Group (VG)
A pooled storage space that aggregates one or more PVs. LVs are created from the free space inside a VG.
Property
Extensible: you can add PVs to increase capacity.
Misconception
VG pooling is not the same as redundancy; LVM alone does not provide RAID-style protection.
Real example
Adding /dev/sdc to a VG that contains /dev/sdb increases available free space so an LV can be extended without downtime when filesystem supports it.
Verification
Use vgdisplay to see VG name, size, and free PE (physical extents) after adding devices.
Analogy
A VG is like a storage pool in a virtual environment. You add disks to the pool and then carve virtual disks from that pool.
Key Takeaway

Use VGs to combine multiple physical devices into a flexible pool. Automate creation and extension with community.general.lvg for repeatable operations.

screens.title: Ansible task: create a Volume Group
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a minimal playbook that creates or extends a Volume Group and implicitly initializes devices as Physical Volumes. The community. general. lvg module takes a vg name and a list of pvs. If the devices are not yet PVs, the module initializes them, creates the VG if missing, or adds the PVs to an existing VG. In automation this removes the need for a separate pvcreate step. Pay attention to idempotency: running the same task again will only change the system if the desired state is not already present. A recommended pattern is to register the module result and then use a debug task to print it so you can see changed/failed status and any returned details. The example playbook shown in the lesson registers lvg_creation_result and then prints it. Practice reading that output to confirm whether the action created a VG, extended one, or made no changes. Always include become: yes for tasks that modify block devices and use careful host targeting so you don't initialize the wrong disks. A common misconception is thinking the module copies data; it does not — it only sets up LVM metadata and membership.

keyIdea.title: Playbook pattern
keyIdea.text: Use community.general.lvg with vg and pvs, register the result, and debug the variable to confirm create/extend actions.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.4 › Ansible playbook
Code example
---
- name: Configure LVM Physical Volumes and Volume Groups
  hosts: lvm_servers
  become: yes
  tasks:
    - name: Ensure /dev/sdb and /dev/sdc are initialized as Physical Volumes and added to 'data_vg'
      community.general.lvg:
        vg: data_vg
        pvs:
          - /dev/sdb
          - /dev/sdc
        state: present
      register: lvg_creation_result

    - name: Display LVM VG creation/extension result
      ansible.builtin.debug:
        var: lvg_creation_result
This task both initializes PVs when needed and creates or extends the named VG in an idempotent way. Registering allows you to inspect what changed.
Walkthrough
  • vg: sets the target Volume Group name, here data_vg.
  • pvs: lists devices to include; lvg will initialize them as PVs if required.
  • state: present ensures the VG exists and the listed PVs are members.
  • register: captures module output to examine changed status and detail.
Key Takeaway

This module simplifies PV initialization and VG creation into a single, repeatable Ansible task. Always inspect the registered output.

screens.title: Safe automation workflow
screens.narratorSegment: A safe workflow for automating PV and VG creation follows three steps: check, run, verify. First, check devices with lsblk to ensure they are the intended targets and are unmounted. This prevents accidental destruction of data. Second, run the Ansible playbook using community. general. lvg to initialize and add devices to the VG. Use become privileges and precise host selection. Third, verify the outcome using pvdisplay and vgdisplay on the managed node to confirm PV headers exist and the VG reflects the expected size. In practice, you will script the check step locally and include ad hoc commands like ansible host -m ansible. builtin. command -a "sudo pvdisplay" to inspect the remote state. A common mistake is skipping the check step or assuming devices are empty; automation magnifies mistakes, so the discipline of verifying before and after is essential. Another helpful practice is to run the Ansible task in a dry-run mode first using check mode where possible, but remember that some changes to block devices are not fully simulated. The final takeaway: adopt the check-run-verify loop in all storage automation to minimize the chance of irreversible device changes.

keyIdea.text: Check device state, run the lvg playbook with become privileges, and verify with pvdisplay/vgdisplay to confirm changes.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.4 › Safe workflow
Step 1
Check
Run lsblk to identify unpartitioned disks and ensure devices are unmounted. Confirm names and availability on the target host.
Step 2
Run
Execute an Ansible playbook using community.general.lvg with become: yes. Register results so you can inspect changed status and module output.
Step 3
Verify
Use pvdisplay and vgdisplay on the managed node to confirm PV headers and VG size. Ensure the free extents match expected capacity.
Common mistake
Adding a device that is mounted or part of another VG will cause errors or data loss. Always unmount and verify device membership first.

screens.title: Idempotency and result inspection
screens.narratorSegment: Idempotency means running an automation task repeatedly produces the same result and only makes changes when the desired state differs from the current state. community. general. lvg is idempotent: if the VG already exists and the PVs are already members, the module reports no changes. This behavior is useful in maintenance pipelines where playbooks run regularly. To understand what happened on a run, register the module output and inspect it with a debug task. The registered result typically contains fields like changed and details about the operation; reading that output tells you whether the module created the VG, extended it, or made no changes. For example, you might see changed: true on the first run and changed: false on subsequent runs if no further devices were added. Be aware that a failed run will return failed: true and an error message that helps diagnose issues such as device-in-use. A concrete example from the chapter registers lvg_creation_result and then prints it; practice making small, easily reversible changes first so you can learn to read module output safely. Key takeaway: rely on idempotency for reliable automation and use registered output to confirm the exact operation performed.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.4 › Idempotency
Concept
Idempotent playbooks
Running the same lvg task multiple times changes the system only if the desired membership or VG state is not already present.
Inspect output
Always register the lvg task result and use a debug task to print changed/failed state and details so you know what modified on the host.
Example registered output
When you register lvg_creation_result and debug it, look for changed: true on the initial run and for any message fields that explain device creation or errors. Use that information to confirm the playbook did exactly what you expected.
Key Takeaway

Idempotency and registered output make automation auditable and safe. Read the module result to verify success and spot failures early.

screens.title: Safety and common mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: Working with block devices carries real risk. The primary safety rule is: verify the device identity and contents before making changes. Initializing a disk as a PV overwrites LVM headers and can destroy metadata or data on the device. Common mistakes include selecting a device that contains a filesystem, adding a device that is already part of another VG, or attempting to add a mounted device. Ansible will usually report errors for these cases, but prevention is better than cure. Use lsblk and other inspection tools to confirm the device is unpartitioned and unmounted. If a disk is part of another VG, either choose a different disk or remove it from that VG intentionally after ensuring data safety. Another useful practice is to tag or label new disks consistently in VM templates so their names are predictable. When in doubt, perform a manual pvdisplay and vgdisplay before automating so you understand the current LVM layout. The key takeaway: automation is powerful, but always pair it with prechecks and verification steps to prevent data loss. Safety and common mistakes means always confirm devices with lsblk and pvdisplay before initializing; never assume a disk is empty without verification.. In practical terms, what can go wrong and how to avoid irreversible changes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Warning › Safety and mistakes
Common mistakes
  • Initializing a device that contains a filesystem and losing data.
  • Attempting to add a device already in another VG without removing it first.
  • Adding a mounted or in-use device, causing errors or corruption.
Preventive actions
  • Run lsblk and confirm the device is unmounted and unpartitioned.
  • Use pvdisplay and vgdisplay to review current LVM state before changes.
  • Label and document VM disk layouts so playbooks target the correct disks.
Safety Note

If you add a disk that already contains data, lvg will overwrite its headers to initialize it as a PV and the previous data will become inaccessible. Always backup critical data before performing block-level operations.

screens.title: Activity: Create a Volume Group from multiple disks
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity walks you through creating a Volume Group from two unpartitioned disks, for example /dev/sdb and /dev/sdc. Step one is to verify disk presence on the target host using lsblk. This confirms device names and mount status. Step two is to write a small playbook that uses community. general. lvg with vg set to the desired name and pvs listing both devices. Make sure to include become: yes so the task has necessary privileges. Step three is to run the playbook using ansible-playbook and register the result to inspect whether the VG was created or extended. Step four is to verify the result remotely with pvdisplay and vgdisplay via Ansible ad-hoc commands or by logging into the managed host. The lesson includes a minimal create_vg. yml playbook as an explicit example that you can adapt. If the run fails because a device is in use, return to the check step and unmount or remove the device from its current VG. This activity ties together the earlier concepts: PV initialization, VG creation or extension, idempotency, and verification. After completing it, reflect on how automation reduced manual steps while still requiring careful prechecks.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.4 › Hands-on
Checklist
  1. Verify disks on the managed node with lsblk.
  2. Create a playbook using community.general.lvg with vg and pvs.
  3. Run ansible-playbook with become privileges and register results.
  4. Verify with pvdisplay and vgdisplay after the run.
Starter playbook
---
- name: Create an LVM Volume Group
  hosts: your_target_host
  become: yes
  tasks:
    - name: Ensure 'app_vg' Volume Group exists and includes /dev/sdb and /dev/sdc
      community.general.lvg:
        vg: app_vg
        pvs:
          - /dev/sdb
          - /dev/sdc
        state: present
      register: vg_status

    - name: Display Volume Group status
      ansible.builtin.debug:
        var: vg_status
Verify
After the playbook runs, confirm with ansible ad-hoc commands or login and run sudo pvdisplay and sudo vgdisplay app_vg to validate that the PVs and VG exist and the capacity is correct.

screens.title: lvg module vs traditional commands
screens.narratorSegment: Automation with community. general. lvg replaces several manual command-line steps with a single declarative task. Traditionally you would run pvcreate for each disk, then vgcreate to form a new Volume Group, or vgextend to add a PV to an existing VG. community. general. lvg handles those steps: when you pass pvs and a vg name, Ansible will initialize the devices as PVs if they are not already and will create or extend the VG as needed. The practical effect is fewer distinct commands to run and lower chance of human error. However, the underlying actions are the same: writing LVM metadata to devices and updating VG membership. A misconception to avoid is thinking the module provides additional safety beyond the commands; it simplifies the workflow but still performs the same destructive operations if devices are incorrect. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we focus on the first layer of LVM automation: turning raw disks into Physical Volumes and grouping them into Volume Groups using Ansible. You will understand what a Physical Volume is, why a Volume Group acts like a pooled storage device, and how Ansible’s community. general. lvg module simplifies creation and extension. We will use concrete playbook examples and show how the module implicitly initializes devices, what idempotent behavior means in practice, and the verification commands used after a run. This matters because managing storage by hand is error-prone; automating LVM saves time and reduces risk when adding capacity, especially across many servers. As you move through the lesson, notice the mapping from raw disks to PVs to a VG to create flexible Logical Volumes later. A common pitfall is initializing a disk that already holds data; we will highlight safety checks and verification steps so you can automate confidently. By the end of this chapter you will be able to write a minimal Ansible task to form a VG from two disks and verify the outcome.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain the three core LVM concepts, create Physical Volumes and Volume Groups using Ansible, extend an existing Volume Group by adding disks, and reason about safety and verification steps. Each objective ties a practical skill to a safety check or verification technique so you automate confidently. For example, you'll learn that marking a disk as a Physical Volume alters its on-disk header, which is why verifying the device with lsblk and pvdisplay is necessary before running a playbook. You will also practice writing a minimal community. general. lvg task that is idempotent and can be run repeatedly without unintended changes. Finally, you will recognize common mistakes such as trying to add a mounted or in-use device, and you will learn the commands to inspect the resulting VG so you can confirm success. These skills let you scale storage changes across many hosts reliably.

This second objectives slide emphasizes practical verification and error recognition. You will learn to read Ansible task results, register the module output, and use simple debug tasks to confirm success. The chapter shows a playbook example where the community. general. lvg result is registered and printed; you'll practice that pattern so you can see whether a VG was created or extended. We'll also cover reading output from pvdisplay and vgdisplay to confirm that the PVs are present and the VG size reflects added disks. Finally, you'll learn to recognize common mistakes: adding a device that belongs to another Volume Group or using a mounted device. Knowing how to read both Ansible results and LVM display commands helps you diagnose and fix issues quickly. This objective ties automation to observability so you don't create silent failures.

A Physical Volume, or PV, is a raw disk or partition that has been prepared for use by LVM. When you initialize a disk as a PV you write an LVM header that identifies the device to the volume management layer; after that the device is not used directly for a traditional filesystem. PVs are the atomic units that Volume Groups pool together. For example, marking /dev/sdb and /dev/sdc as PVs allows you to combine their capacity into a single VG. This is useful when a single filesystem needs more capacity than a single disk. A common misconception is that a PV is a filesystem or mountable device — it is not. It is an LVM-managed block that must be part of a VG to host a Logical Volume. A practical example: you discover two unpartitioned disks on a VM. You run an Ansible task that references those devices; the community. general. lvg module will initialize them as PVs if necessary. Always verify devices with lsblk or pvdisplay before automating to avoid overwriting important data. Key takeaway: PVs convert physical disks or partitions into LVM-managed capacity and are the first step in creating flexible, resizable volumes.

A Volume Group, or VG, aggregates one or more Physical Volumes into a single storage pool. Think of a VG as a virtual super-disk: it exposes the combined capacity of its member PVs so you can create Logical Volumes of arbitrary size up to the total free space. This pooling is the key advantage of LVM because it lets you grow storage for an application without being constrained to single physical disks. For example, if you add /dev/sdc to an existing VG that already includes /dev/sdb, the VG capacity increases and you can extend LVs carved from it. An important property is that VGs are extensible: adding PVs increases total free space. Another practical note is that operations against VGs in automation should be idempotent; Ansible's community. general. lvg module will create the VG if missing and add devices that are not yet members. Remember that adding a PV to a VG writes to the device header, so the safety checks for PVs apply here as well. Finally, a misconception is thinking a VG automatically balances data across disks in the same way as RAID; LVM pools capacity but does not provide redundancy unless configured with mirroring or higher-level replication. Key takeaway: VGs give you a single namespace for capacity and make resizing and allocation far simpler.

Let's walk through a minimal playbook that creates or extends a Volume Group and implicitly initializes devices as Physical Volumes. The community. general. lvg module takes a vg name and a list of pvs. If the devices are not yet PVs, the module initializes them, creates the VG if missing, or adds the PVs to an existing VG. In automation this removes the need for a separate pvcreate step. Pay attention to idempotency: running the same task again will only change the system if the desired state is not already present. A recommended pattern is to register the module result and then use a debug task to print it so you can see changed/failed status and any returned details. The example playbook shown in the lesson registers lvg_creation_result and then prints it. Practice reading that output to confirm whether the action created a VG, extended one, or made no changes. Always include become: yes for tasks that modify block devices and use careful host targeting so you don't initialize the wrong disks. A common misconception is thinking the module copies data; it does not — it only sets up LVM metadata and membership.

A safe workflow for automating PV and VG creation follows three steps: check, run, verify. First, check devices with lsblk to ensure they are the intended targets and are unmounted. This prevents accidental destruction of data. Second, run the Ansible playbook using community. general. lvg to initialize and add devices to the VG. Use become privileges and precise host selection. Third, verify the outcome using pvdisplay and vgdisplay on the managed node to confirm PV headers exist and the VG reflects the expected size. In practice, you will script the check step locally and include ad hoc commands like ansible host -m ansible. builtin. command -a "sudo pvdisplay" to inspect the remote state. A common mistake is skipping the check step or assuming devices are empty; automation magnifies mistakes, so the discipline of verifying before and after is essential. Another helpful practice is to run the Ansible task in a dry-run mode first using check mode where possible, but remember that some changes to block devices are not fully simulated. The final takeaway: adopt the check-run-verify loop in all storage automation to minimize the chance of irreversible device changes.

Idempotency means running an automation task repeatedly produces the same result and only makes changes when the desired state differs from the current state. community. general. lvg is idempotent: if the VG already exists and the PVs are already members, the module reports no changes. This behavior is useful in maintenance pipelines where playbooks run regularly. To understand what happened on a run, register the module output and inspect it with a debug task. The registered result typically contains fields like changed and details about the operation; reading that output tells you whether the module created the VG, extended it, or made no changes. For example, you might see changed: true on the first run and changed: false on subsequent runs if no further devices were added. Be aware that a failed run will return failed: true and an error message that helps diagnose issues such as device-in-use. A concrete example from the chapter registers lvg_creation_result and then prints it; practice making small, easily reversible changes first so you can learn to read module output safely. Key takeaway: rely on idempotency for reliable automation and use registered output to confirm the exact operation performed.

Working with block devices carries real risk. The primary safety rule is: verify the device identity and contents before making changes. Initializing a disk as a PV overwrites LVM headers and can destroy metadata or data on the device. Common mistakes include selecting a device that contains a filesystem, adding a device that is already part of another VG, or attempting to add a mounted device. Ansible will usually report errors for these cases, but prevention is better than cure. Use lsblk and other inspection tools to confirm the device is unpartitioned and unmounted. If a disk is part of another VG, either choose a different disk or remove it from that VG intentionally after ensuring data safety. Another useful practice is to tag or label new disks consistently in VM templates so their names are predictable. When in doubt, perform a manual pvdisplay and vgdisplay before automating so you understand the current LVM layout. The key takeaway: automation is powerful, but always pair it with prechecks and verification steps to prevent data loss. Safety and common mistakes means always confirm devices with lsblk and pvdisplay before initializing; never assume a disk is empty without verification..
